Interchanging hyperfunction integration and analytic substitution

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

Contracting two kernels produces another kernel. To identify its action with two successive actions, integration must commute with an admitted singular product. We prove the stronger underlying fact: noncharacteristic analytic substitution commutes with proper fiber integration. It applies at critical points of the analytic map as well as at regular points.

The proof retains the compact analytic-functional construction of hyperfunctions. A contour is kept fixed at the fiber boundary. The remaining carrier ambiguity then lies only over the boundary of the output patch. Exponential decay permits a later deformation over the whole fiber. No finite distributional order is required.

Write . All scalar integrals use Lebesgue density in the fiber coordinates. We use the complete compact-carrier, boundary and operation proofs listed at the end.

Integrating holomorphic sides with canceling tails

We record a precise situation in which individual holomorphic sides may be integrated even though their hyperfunction boundaries need not have proper support individually.

Let be holomorphic on uniform wedges over , with open convex joint approach cones . Work locally on relatively compact base sets. Assume:

  1. Every continues across the real region , with a common complex collar in the base and bounded fiber imaginary coordinates.
  2. On the fiber tails, every fixed derivative has a bound uniformly on each of the compact base and bounded imaginary parameter sets used below.
  3. The real tail continuations cancel: An ordinary holomorphic summand is permitted. Its boundary is its analytic trace.

Let be the projection of to the base imaginary coordinates. If , interpret the integrated side below as an ordinary holomorphic germ near the real base. Otherwise is an open convex cone not containing zero.

Theorem 2 (integration of a canceling family). The hyperfunction has support proper over . Its proper integral is where is any sufficiently small admissible lift in . The value is independent of that lift.

Proof: the integrated sides. For a fixed admissible lift, (I1) gives absolute convergence, locally uniform with every fixed derivative. It follows by local power series, or the supplied Cauchy formula, that the integral is holomorphic in . If two fiber heights have the same base imaginary coordinate, their segment is in the convex cone. Shift fiber coordinates on finite rectangles and use (C4), or one-variable Cauchy integration. Their remote faces are bounded by a polynomial in their radius times , which tends to zero. Thus the two integrals agree. These local definitions glue.

Projection of an open convex set under a linear projection is open and convex: a small ball about each lift projects onto a base ball. Compact subsets of projected directions have finitely many such lift neighborhoods, with bounded lifts. This gives the uniform small heights required for a -holomorphic germ. If , fix a lift ; openness gives a full complex base neighborhood on which the same fiber height works. The output is then an ordinary holomorphic germ.

The tail traces in (I2) make zero outside a fixed fiber ball on each base patch. Its support is therefore proper there, and hence proper over .

On , Lemma 1 identifies the sum with . The extra carrier in (I5) lies over ; elsewhere the fiber support is compactly inside . Thus agrees with over and every fiber point, including the prescribed zeros outside . The actual proper integral on is the class of , by Integrating hyperfunctions over proper fibers, Theorem 2.

Proof: a deformation over the entire fiber. Pair with an entire output test . Extend the finite fiber integral to . The added summed integral is zero by (I2). For each summand separately deform Where , the positive multiple of is admissible; the tail continuation handles its zero values. All derivatives of the graph coefficients are bounded. Apply (C4) first on a large fiber box. The fiber-face integrals tend to zero by (I1), even after their polynomial area factor. For the base faces use the same base-collar subtraction and Cauchy bounds as in Lemma 1. Their fiber integrals are finite by (I1), with a bounded finite part. Thus the difference between the two endpoints is carried by This is an exact carrier estimate for each fixed ; its constant may depend on .

At , the determinant is one. Absolute fiber integration gives If , this is the translated-test representative used to define . If , it is the ordinary real integral of the analytic output. The boundary theorem compares it with a compact output representative modulo a carrier shrinking to .

Finally (C3), after projection, also has carrier shrinking to . Projection of a complex carrier is legitimate here directly: the pairing is with , and a neighborhood of the projected compact set pulls back to a neighborhood of the original carrier. Combining these comparisons for every sufficiently small puts the fixed difference in , where are the output representatives. Their hyperfunctions therefore agree on . Gluing proves (I4).

The cancellation was used before discarding the fiber boundary. Integrating arbitrary angular pieces as individually proper hyperfunctions would not justify this argument.

A singular projection formula

Proposition 4 (independent factors and singular multipliers). Tensoring with an independent hyperfunction commutes with proper integration. Moreover, if is proper over and satisfies then

Proof. On compact representatives, tensoring with an independent factor and then integrating pairs the tensor functional with exactly the same entire test as integrating first and then tensoring. The full iterated germ-pairing identity is Analytic tests and real carriers, Proposition 7. The whole-fiber compact representatives of the integration lesson identify these compact formulas with the actual proper operations; locality glues them.

To prove (P2), use independent base variables and form . Its support is proper over . The base diagonal has nonzero normal . For its product with the fiber identity, the normal is . The full tensor bound shows that such a normal is excluded exactly by (P1); neither support-zero component alone can produce it. Theorem 3 commutes this pullback with fiber integration. Independent-factor integration gives before pullback. Tensor naturality and the definition of the diagonal product give the two sides of (P2). The proper-integral wavefront bound also directly admits the left product; the right product's support is a closed subset of the original proper support.

Entire chains of kernels

Let , . Use the support-extended primed relation from Singular inputs and zero covectors in hyperfunction kernels: For each contiguous block , let be the set of all compatible base tuples whose -th adjacent pair lies in . Require:

  • is proper over its exterior variables .
  • At every tuple in , a path in the extended relations with zero exterior covectors is trivial: For a block of length one both requirements are automatic. Every interior may be zero; the condition excludes only a nontrivial path with zero ends.

Theorem 5 (finite contraction and associativity). Under these assumptions every parenthesization of the kernel chain is defined, and all give the same kernel Here the product is the simultaneous tensor restriction to the compatible-variable diagonal. It has the full bound The right side is locally closed off the joint exterior zero.

Proof: the direct construction. The full tensor bound retains a support zero for each factor. The transpose of the compatible-variable diagonal adds the two raw covector components at each common variable. In primed notation its kernel consists exactly of paths in (K2). Thus (K2) makes this pullback noncharacteristic. Outside the tensor is zero near the image point, so there is no extra condition there. The restricted section has support in ; its assumed properness permits (K3).

The pullback and integration bounds require equality of adjacent primed covectors, while leaving the exterior pair nonzero. They give exactly (K4). Properness bounds the interior base variables over compact exterior sets. If interior covectors in a convergent exterior sequence were unbounded, divide the entire path by their largest norm and pass to a subsequence. Closedness of each extended relation would give a nontrivial path with zero ends, contrary to (K2). Otherwise take a bounded subsequence and pass to its limit. This proves the asserted closedness, including all zero interior components.

Proof: every intermediate contraction is admitted. A contracted block's nonzero relation lies in its full path relation by (K4). At a support zero of that block, its support inclusion supplies a compatible raw base tuple; assign zero covectors to all its factors. Thus its extended relation also lifts to a raw path. A forbidden opposite pair when two adjacent blocks are contracted would lift to a nontrivial raw path with zero exterior covectors for their union. Condition (K2) excludes it.

Their joint support is proper over the exterior variables: each block support lies in the projection of its raw support, whose projection is closed by properness. A compatible pair of block support points lifts to one raw tuple for their union. Hence the joint support is a closed subset of the corresponding compact projection of over any compact exterior set. This proves the required properness at every cut.

Proof: equality with one direct integral. Split a block into two adjacent blocks. Their unintegrated restricted tensors multiply to the restricted tensor of the whole block. To check this factorization, use tensor naturality and pullback functoriality; any forbidden normal at an intermediate product would, after summing the internal components and putting its unused components equal to zero, be a forbidden path in (K2). Thus every map used in the factorization is admitted.

An unintegrated block is proper over its two exterior variables. After adjoining the other variables it remains proper over the enlarged base. Apply Proposition 4 to move its integration through multiplication by the other block. Its exclusion (P1) is again precisely a nontrivial raw path with zero ends: a covector killed in that integration has zero components in the integrated variables, and the opposite product covector supplies the remaining matching components. Condition (K2) excludes it. Apply the same argument to the other block.

The total restricted tensor has support proper over the final exterior variables. The full repeated-integration theorem in the integration lesson, Proposition 7, now identifies these successive integrations and the remaining common-variable integral with (K3). Induction on block length proves that every binary parenthesization equals that direct expression. No continuity argument through smooth approximants is used.

A familiar sufficient properness hypothesis is that is proper over its input for every . Starting from a compact final input set and proceeding backwards bounds all interior variables; the first exterior variable is already in a compact set. The theorem permits the more general joint properness stated above.

Corollary 6 (composed action). Regard as a terminal kernel from to a point. If satisfy the block properness and no-zero-path conditions above, then This includes arbitrary admissible singular inputs. Compact support of and properness of over ensure all the required support conditions. For noncompact inputs the exact joint properness conditions suffice.

Proof. The terminal extended relation is the wavefront of with its support zero, followed by the zero cotangent space of the point. The two length-two block conditions admit and . The length-three condition admits both remaining actions. Theorem 5 identifies their parenthesizations. In the compact-input sufficient case, compactness bounds , properness of then bounds , and compact output sets bound . The respective closed support sets are therefore compact.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 (basic) — the boundary that survives. In Lemma 1, explain why replacing by the full boundary of would not suffice after projection.

Solution. The full boundary contains , whose projection contains the whole . A functional carried there can give a nonzero output in the interior. For example , with and compact nonzero supported inside , projects to . In contrast, , so a functional carried by gives the zero hyperfunction on . The vanishing inserted-column factors near the fiber faces are the exact reason the smaller carrier is available.

Exercise 2 (intermediate) — substitution at a critical point. Let and . Compute both sides of Theorem 3, including at .

Solution. The support is the diagonal, proper over , and its exact wavefront consists of nonzero multiples of . No nonzero covector has fiber component zero. Thus (B1) holds even where . The pullback is , by the analytic coordinate change in the fiber, whose fiber Jacobian is one. Each fiber integral is one. Hence both sides are the analytic function .

The same example works beyond distributions. Let The moment theorem and the finite-jet argument supplied in the preceding lessons prove that is a nonzero point-supported hyperfunction of infinite order, with all nonzero directions. Exact submersion and coordinate covariance again give only diagonal conormals. Its fiber integral is ; after substitution it is with the same integral. The map remains admissible at its critical point.

Exercise 3 (basic) — properness alone does not admit a restriction. Let and let be the constant map with value zero.

Solution. The support is compact, but at the origin is the full punctured joint fiber. In particular it contains for , and . Condition (B1) fails. The output integral is , whose pullback by the constant map is likewise not admitted by the noncharacteristic construction. Theorem 3 asserts no value for either forbidden restriction.

Exercise 4 (intermediate) — a singular multiplier through a point fiber. For an arbitrary hyperfunction , let . Verify Proposition 4 directly.

Solution. Its support is proper over . Its only nonzero wavefront covectors are pure fiber covectors, so (P1) holds for every . The product is , by tensor and diagonal compatibility. Compact germ pairing and localization give and . This proves (P2) here even when has no finite distributional order.

Exercise 5 (intermediate) — a zero middle covector and a noncompact input. On three real lines take Compute both composed actions and check the support conditions.

Solution. One has , , and , giving the same action on . These are the actual tensor and point-evaluation pairings. The support is , proper over ; the other joint supports have the relevant interior variables fixed at zero. Thus every block is proper although is not compactly supported. The input has empty wavefront. A zero-ended path first forces the input covector to zero, then its output covector to zero, and then the input covector to zero. Condition (K2) follows. The contracted kernel retains the full punctured outer fiber, including paths whose middle covector is zero.

Exercise 6 (intermediate) — an arbitrary translation chain. Set . Determine every contraction of a finite chain.

Solution. Each support is a translation graph, proper over either endpoint. Its primed relation equates its two covectors. A compatible path therefore has all covectors equal; zero exterior covectors force the whole path to zero. Theorem 5 applies. Integrating a delta in the last graph variable has coefficient one, so induction gives No absolute scaling factor arises because each eliminated variable has coefficient or . The theorem proves equality for all parenthesizations, not just this order of evaluation.

Exercise 7 (advanced) — adjacent exclusions do not settle a triple. Take Check adjacent contractions and find the full-chain obstruction.

Solution. The graph kernel has neither a nonzero input-axis nor a nonzero output-axis covector. Thus each adjacent pair meets the two-kernel exclusion. The pair contractions are and . But the full raw chain has paths in its extended primed relations, over . They violate (K2). Either attempted final contraction encounters opposite nonzero covectors in its common variable. All support properness conditions hold; it is the wavefront condition that fails. The canonical operations proved here do not assign a triple contraction in this case.

Exercise 8 (basic) — empty wavefront and an infinite fiber. Let on products of real lines. Explain why Theorem 5 does not assert their contraction.

Solution. There are no nonzero wavefront covectors, so the path condition holds. The raw support is all . Over a fixed outer point the middle fiber is the whole line, which is not compact. Properness fails, and the formal integral of over that fiber diverges. An empty wavefront cannot replace the support condition.
